sources.title: Zambia National Heritage Conservation Commission: Barotse Cultural Landscape, 2009 tentative submission
sources.note: State-party tentative-list description, not an inscription on the World Heritage List. Directly read: canals, settlement mounds, weirs, Lealui and Lewanika chronology.

sources.title: British Museum: Lozi lidded bowl, Af1902,0513.18.a
sources.note: Official indexed collection record fully read; direct fetch failed. Date about 1891 to 1901; six swimming ducks; historical label restricts use to headmen. Curatorial discussion distinguishes Lozi court from contributing Kwangwa and Mbunda carvers.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum: Lozi lidded basket, 2021.225a, b
sources.note: Direct collection record: about 1900 to 1920, Makenge root fibre and pigment, women’s coiled baskets, overseas market and animal designs.

sources.title: Jack Hogan: The ends of slavery in Barotseland, Western Zambia, 2014
sources.note: University of Kent doctoral archival research, directly accessible. Abstract, chapters 7 to 9 and appendices: exploited labour in public works, formal abolition 1906, continued bondage and unpaid labour.

sources.title: Peggy Mwanza: The Role of Non-Governmental Organisations in Basic Education Policy Reform in Lusaka Province of Zambia, 2013
sources.note: University of Edinburgh doctoral study, printed 17: Barotse National School opened March 1907, seven pupils, agreement to use ten percent of tax revenue; cites Snelson 1974.

sources.title: Lee Bickmore and Kristina Riedel: Silozi Phrasal Tonology, 2025
sources.note: Authors’ full article text read, DOI 10.53228/s0e4bp10; printed 246 elicitation with Mubiana Liswaniso in 2022 to 2024, printed 264 example 48(c). Latin orthography with scholarly tones and morpheme hyphens retained.

sources.title: Zambia Department of Water Affairs: Environmental and social impact assessment for Barotse canals, 2015
sources.note: World Bank-hosted government project report; official indexed Water Sources and Sanitation sections read, direct fetch failed. Modern conditions explicitly separated from nineteenth century.

sources.title: UK Parliament: Clause 8, agreements relating to Barotseland, 10 July 1964
sources.note: Direct parliamentary debate; John Tilney’s ministerial explanation of replacement of Crown/company agreements and Barotseland as part of unitary Zambia. Negotiators’ optimistic opinions not treated as proof of later compliance.

sources.title: Andrew Reid: The emergence of states in Great Lakes Africa, 2013
sources.note: Publisher abstract directly read: Nkore among Great Lakes states, local state formation, thin and partial archaeological record. No detailed excavated findings inferred from abstract.

sources.title: Andrew Reid and Peter Robertshaw: A new look at Ankole capital sites, 1987
sources.note: Bibliographic abstract checked: 1987 visits to sites associated in oral tradition with particular Bagabe; potential for excavation, not completed excavation. DOI 10.1080/00672708709511383.

sources.title: John Roscoe: The Northern Bantu, 1915, Banyankole chapters
sources.note: Full public-domain text mirror directly read. Printed 105 housing and water troughs; printed 113 princely education. Colonial outsider with prejudiced racial theory; only specified concrete observations used and attributed, not his generalizations.

sources.title: Igongo Cultural Centre Museum: collection catalogue, 2012
sources.note: Direct 28-page catalogue, museum staff interviews dated 22 March 2012. Item 1 churning gourd; 2 pot-smoking equipment; 7 herders’ trumpet; 8 water pot with Runyankore label; 20 stretcher. Object dates are not supplied; modern documentation is explicit.

sources.title: D. A. Low: Fabrication of Empire, 2009, chapter summaries
sources.note: Direct publisher extracts for chapters 8, 10 and 11. Nkore independence, British domination 1898 to 1901, Mbaguta and enlargement of colonial Ankole. Not whole book access.

sources.title: Ankole Agreement, signed 25 October 1901, reproduced text
sources.note: Full primary treaty transcription on community history site; text checked. Independent university library catalog confirms document, but reproduction includes typographical errors. Use substantive clauses, not exact original handwriting.

sources.title: Cambridge Museum of Archaeology and Anthropology: Repositioning the Uganda Museum, 2021
sources.note: Direct museum report on collections, acquisition routes and proposed return on loan; distinguish its described project stage from later completion.

sources.title: Uganda High Commission: History and political situation
sources.note: Official indexed history: 1967 abolition of monarchies under Obote. No claim that every kingdom’s present status is the same.

sources.title: François-Xavier Fauvelle, Bertrand Hirsch and Amélie Chekroun: Le sultanat de l’Awfāt, 2017
sources.note: Complete author PDF directly read. Printed 243: Makhzumi dynasty ended in 1285 and places in its annals remain unidentified. Printed 270 to 272: tomb T9, Arabic transcription by Julien Loiseau and French translation; dated 23 April to 3 May 1364. Text extraction verified, PDF screenshot unavailable. Later Ifat context must not become an inscription assigned to the earlier Shewa sultanate.

sources.title: François-Xavier Fauvelle and Romain Mensan: Nora excavation synthesis, 2024
sources.note: Direct chapter 10 PDF, printed 195 to 197. Latest synthesis distinguishes medieval rectilinear houses from later undated curvilinear buildings; surrounding reservoirs and terraces not securely medieval. Local rhyolite and ignimbrite, clay floors and ovens, grinding equipment.

sources.title: Helina Solomon Woldekiros: Animal utilization at the medieval Islamic site of Nora, 2024
sources.note: Direct chapter 8 PDF. Printed 153 recovery by hand without screening; 156 to 157 cut marks and cattle age; 161 to 162 interpretation. Old cattle may indicate milk and traction. No unsupported inference about fish absence or whole-city diet.

sources.title: Stéphane Pradines: The Medieval Mosques of Nora, 2017
sources.note: Direct full article. Printed 50 to 51: M2 mosque, about 19 square metres, central roof column and basalt stone interpreted as an ablution footrest. Specific interpretation retained; broader early housing chronology superseded by 2024 synthesis.

sources.title: Beatriz Marín-Aguilera and Laure Dussubieux: The Allure of Glass Beads, 2023
sources.note: Direct original laboratory study. Shay communities distinct from Christian and Muslim neighbours; Məsḥalä Māryām Tumulus 2 grave assemblage and study of 34 beads. Glass chemistry indicates raw-material provenance, not necessarily bead-making location or a direct voyage.

sources.title: Timothy Insoll: The archaeology of complexity and cosmopolitanism in medieval Ethiopia, 2021
sources.note: Publisher article and indexed official PDF, printed 459, checked. Christian mobile camps, possible Menz camp and Meshala Maryam Raphael church. Article’s apparent 1448 typo in Baeda Maryam reign not reproduced; fifteenth century used. Regional synthesis does not establish exact imported Shoa identity.

proposedOverrides.name: Shoa (medieval Shewa region)
proposedOverrides.summary: Medieval Shewa’s varied communities, explored through named sites and carefully distinguished political phases.

batchIdentityNotes.note: Import explicitly points to Lozi kingdom. Polygon lies north of Lealui (about 15.22 S) and much of core floodplain; public warning retained. No modern sovereignty inference. Modern writing and water examples dated; 1964 framework does not claim subsequent compliance.

Major western displacement and mismatch with Mbarara area publicly acknowledged. Precolonial Nkore separate from enlarged colonial Ankole. Later ethnography and museum witnesses dated explicitly. No claim that Igongo objects are nineteenth-century artifacts.

Imported polygon is far northeast of Shewa sites; identity unresolved between broad regional label and medieval sultanate. Public opening makes this explicit. Do not claim uninterrupted Makhzumi state to 1492, do not substitute nineteenth-century Shoa, and do not assign Ifat or Shay artifacts to Makhzumi rulers. Writing is explicitly a later Ifat contextual witness.
